title: Giving meaning to marks
keyIdea: Marks on paper can say something. A scribble becomes writing when you say what it means: this says Nana, this is my shopping list. Writing looks different from a picture: small marks in a line. Each paper has a job, we read from the top and from the left, and the marks say the same thing every time.
familyTip: Leave paper and crayons where you write your own lists and cards. When your child makes marks, ask: What does it say? Write their words under the marks, and read it back together the next day.

visual.caption: Is it a picture or writing? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Mia's name on her coat peg

lab.caption: Flagship lab: make marks and say what they mean, sort pictures from writing, give each paper its job, write Sam's name, read a list and a card back.

kid: You can make marks with a crayon. Big ones, small ones, wiggly ones.
Your marks can say something. Mia makes three wiggles and says: This says milk, eggs, bread. That is her shopping list!
Writing is small marks in a line. A picture shows a thing, like a sun or a cat.
When you read your marks again, they say the same thing. Start at the top, and go from left to right.
adult: Ages 3 to 4. Development Matters (2021) Literacy says children from birth to 3 add some marks to their drawings, which they give meaning to ('That says mummy'), and children aged 3 to 4 use some of their print and letter knowledge in early writing, such as a pretend shopping list that starts at the top of the page, or writing 'm' for mummy. It also names the concepts about print: print has meaning, print has different purposes, and English is read from left to right and top to bottom. Key words: mark-making, emergent writing, letter-like shapes, concepts about print.

Model writing for real reasons: lists, cards, labels and signs. Give your child the same job: write a list for the shop, a card for a friend, a sign for their door. Ask what their marks say, and accept any answer. Write their words underneath so they see the link between talk and print.

Common mistakes: grown-ups dismiss scribbles as just a mess, so the child stops trying; a child thinks a picture of a cat is the word cat; reading a list from the bottom up; and a reading that changes each time. Be careful not to push neat letters too soon: meaning comes first, letters follow, often starting with the letters in the child's own name.

In the lab your child draws marks and says what they mean, sorts pictures from writing, gives a list, card, label and sign to the place that needs each one, writes Sam's name from S, A and M, and reads a list from the top and a card from the left.

practice.prompt: Mia's shopping list has {n} lines of marks. Each line says one thing to buy. How many things does she need?
practice.hint: One line says one thing. Count the lines.
practice.explain: Each line says one thing, and there are {n} lines, so Mia needs {n} things.

practice.prompt: Mia has {n} toys to take to Nana's house. She makes one mark on her list for each toy. How many marks does her list need?
practice.hint: One mark stands for one toy. Count the toys.
practice.explain: One mark for each toy, and she has {n} toys, so her list needs {n} marks.

practice.prompt: Leo makes some wiggles on a card. He says: This says Happy birthday Nana. Is it writing?
choices: No, it is just a mess
practice.hint: Did Leo say what his marks say?
practice.explain: Leo gave his marks a meaning. That is how writing starts.

practice.prompt: Which paper do you take to the shop?
practice.hint: Which paper says what to buy?
practice.explain: A shopping list says what to buy. A card says hello, and a sign tells people what to do.

practice.prompt: Where do you start to read a list?
practice.hint: Mia wrote milk first, at the top.
practice.explain: A list starts at the top and goes down, one line at a time.

pool.hint: Writing is not a picture of a thing.
pool.explain: Writing is small marks in a line, like letters. A sun and a house are pictures.

pool.prompt: What is a sign on a bedroom door for?
choices: To tell people what to do, like Keep out
pool.hint: Who reads a sign on a door?
pool.explain: A sign tells people what to do. Each paper has its own job.

pool.prompt: Sam writes S on his picture. What might it say?
pool.hint: S is the first letter of his own name.
pool.explain: S is the first letter of Sam. Children often write letters from their own name first.

pool.prompt: Mia reads her list again the next day. What does it say?
choices: The same as before: milk, eggs, bread
pool.hint: Do marks change what they say?
pool.explain: Marks keep their meaning. Her list says milk, eggs, bread every time.

pool.prompt: Mia's card has {n} marks in a line. Which mark do you read first?
pool.hint: We read along a line from one side to the other.
pool.explain: We read from left to right, so start with the mark on the left, then read all {n} marks along the line.

pool.prompt: Leo makes a card. He writes {n} kisses: x for each kiss. How many x marks are on the card?
pool.hint: One x stands for one kiss.
pool.explain: Each x means one kiss. {n} kisses need {n} x marks.

pool.prompt: A child makes some marks. What is a good thing for a grown-up to ask?
pool.explain: Asking what it says shows the child that marks carry meaning.

pool.prompt: Which paper says whose bag it is?
pool.hint: What do you put on a bag or a peg?
pool.explain: A name label says who owns the bag. Many children first write their name for this job.

pool.prompt: Mia reads her list: bread, eggs, milk. She wrote milk at the top. What was her slip?
choices: She read from the bottom; start at the top
pool.hint: Where does a list start? Look at which word is at the top.
pool.explain: Milk is at the top, so the list reads milk, eggs, bread. Start at the top.
